ALLEGED MISLEADING ADVERTISEMENT CONCERNING STABILIZATION BILL AND WHEAT RESERVES ACT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask for unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion in a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
This matter concerns a full-page presentation which appeared in the Saturday, October 2, issue of the Regina Leader-Post. This sheet is headed by the familiar exhortation, "It's your choice", which is followed by the equally familiar nostrum that is composed in equal parts of a suppression of the truth and a suggestion of the false. The subject matter is the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and the prairie grain stabilization bill-a subject matter that is now before this House as well as before the courts. The blurb purports to be authorized by the "Keep the Stabilization Plan Committee". The seriously disturbing fact in this fiction is the assertion that the stabilization plan is endorsed by a farm organization which has since denied such endorsation. That assertion, in a matter before the House and the courts, is serious.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta):
That the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs inquire into the advertisement which appeared in the Leader-Post of the 2nd October, 1971, concerning the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and the prairie grain stabilization bill with respect to the misleading allegations therein contained and report back to this House.

Mr. Speaker, just before ten o'clock last evening, I was explaining to the House, at some length, the reason for our opposition to this bill as it now stands. This is related largely to the fact that it is based upon considerations of gross farm income rather than net farm income. Over a period of years that fact would mean that the bill would have the effect of accelerating the process of forcing the small farmer off the land, thereby altering the whole cultural pattern of western Canada and its whole way of life. I was suggesting that the social consequences of such legislation had not been taken into account by the government. They should be and that is why we are fighting so hard to have this change made.
This morning when reading a speech made by the hon. I recognize quite readily that if Bill C-244 passes, in addition to the fact that the farmers would have $65 million in their pockets in this three-year period as opposed to $113 million under the present law, there would be in the stabilization fund a total of $105 million which would be made up of the $70 million put in it in the two years by the government and the $35 million put in by the farmers. I have had so many letters over the years from retired public service employees and retired CNR employees and others wondering why they could not get the benefit of the millions of dollars in funds that I do not want the farmers put in the position where they can be told they are well off because there is this huge amount of money in the stabilization fund most of which they may never see.

I have done so because of what the government has done and what the Prime Minister did the other night in the dishonest and distorted picture he gave when he talked about this $113 million. I think the figure was $112 point something million, but the minister says $113 million and that is about the same. The Prime Minister said, leave the legislation as it is; let the opposition deny us the right to pass this bill and that is all the farmers get, $113 million, in these three years, but pass the bill a generous Liberal government has brought in and they will have $170 million. This is not true. They will have a net of $65 million under Bill C-244 as opposed to $113 million under the present law.
That leads us to the question of the stabilization fund, the $105 million that would be there at the end of two years if the government's calculations are correct. This goes to the whole question of the rationale of this bill and our reason for trying to improve it. That is what the amendments before us now are all about-the motion of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) and the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). The whole purpose of these amendments is to try to improve the formula in this bill which provides for the farmers to get payments from the fund.
It is no improvement in the farmer's position and no fun just to put money into a fund all their lives. There is a possibility that is what could happen because this fund

This is not a stabilization program. At best it is an income insurance program for a year of disaster, a year of catastrophe. I submit it is not properly drawn. It is not even a good insurance scheme. I think the more the farmers come to understand it the more they feel it should not be pushed down their throats. That is why we are opposing it in the course of this debate as we are. Last June there was some opposition to it. My friend sitting behind me and I were accused of blocking it. We accept the accusation and the disastrous political result because we like the kind of disaster which took place in Saskatchewan on June 23. Why did the farmers of Saskatchewan vote against the Liberals? For quite a few reasons, but one is that they do not like the so-called stabilization plan. The effect of this stabilization plan, if it does anything, is to stabilize poverty. You know, Mr. Speaker, this government is awfully good at this job of redistributing poverty. You would stop me if I got too far into the matter of old age pensions but I will not go so far that you will have to stop me.
What happened the last time the government amended the old age security act? It redistributed the poverty of the old people. It took some away from some old people to give a little more to other old people. The government is good at redistributing poverty. The government tells us that this legislation will make things better. The Minister of Supply and Services said that this is an improvement and that is why we in western Canada should support it. We were told about the new unemployment insurance act, that it was a tremendous improvement. Not a day passes that I do not receive letters from people saying that they are worse off under it than they were before. Some people are better off, but some people are worse off. We were told the same thing about the veterans legislation. How many members receive letters, particularly from those on the war veterans allowance, who state that their position has been made most difficult because of the way that act operates. So, we do not accept the assertion of the Minister of Supply and Services or of the government that this legislation is an improvement over the old one and therefore we are not being filibusterers, obstructionists, undemocratic and irresponsible because we oppose this legislation. We are not just playing around with it and making amendments for the fun of it. We say it is a bad bill. We say that it is against the interests of the farmers of
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
western Canada and that it should not be supported by this House.
You might say, Mr. Speaker, when are you going to talk about the amendment? Let me talk about it enough to be in order, but to this point I have been dealing with the remarks made by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson).
The point of the motion and amendment is to try to improve the bill a little so that there will be some chance of the farmers getting some money out of this fund into which they will have to pay money if this bill passes. But the way the bill now reads, the farmers can get income out of the fund only if the total gross income with respect to the six grains that are dealt with in this bill is below the average of the immediately preceding five years. We contend that that figure of gross income is a misleading one, particularly because of the rising costs of production that can take place and there is no chance of farmers gaining from this unless the income in a bad year is at least the net income.
That was the purpose of the motion moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave). Under this motion, when the net income, rather than the gross income, falls below the average of the preceding five years, payments would come into effect. The purpose of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) is to be somewhat more precise and to set the first crop year in this cycle as the base period and to take into account the increased cost of production between that base year and subsequent years. We think that that would make at least a slight improvement, that there would be some chance of there being years in which farmers would get benefits out of the fund.
That is why we think the House should support the amendment and then support the motion as amended by the words in the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena. But I have no hesitation in saying that even if that takes place, the bill is still not a stabilization plan; it is not what the ministers over there talk about, namely, something that will even out the bumps and the hollows. It is at best a plan to provide income insurance for years that are particularly bad, particularly catastrophic. We may go 10 or 20 years without having that kind of year, particularly because of this so-called moving average. I say, therefore, that even if this bill were amended it would not be the kind of bill that would meet the situation. One of the difficulties is that if you get this kind of bill on the statute books, as with so many other things, it will be years before it can be changed. I say to the Minister of Supply and Services, my neighbour from Winnipeg, that I think we would be rendering a disservice to the farmers of western Canada if we allowed this bill to pass. That is why we are still standing here doing our best to persuade the government to withdraw it.
I continue to protest against the failure of the government to carry out the law as it now obtains in the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act which requires these payments to be made. The government is now 15 months in default, and the law is there just as much for the government as it is for anyone else, and it has not been kept.

I also object very strongly to the fact that this debate is taking place during the early days of this week after the clear understanding that was arrived at between the minister and the prairie ministers of agriculture last Friday that there would be a moratorium, a cooling off period, during which the government would look at the proposals made to it by those ministers. You cannot call it consideration just to have slept on it over the weekend from Friday to Monday.
I have no hesitation in saying that I have been speaking to at least one of the western ministers of agriculture and he was horrified to learn yesterday that this bill was under debate. I tried to explain, but he certainly had the clear understanding that the bill would not be proceeded with until the minister in charge of the Wheat Board had reported back to the western ministers of agriculture. I am told that the minister's assistant has communicated with at least one minister to inform him that the debate was on again, but there has been no answer to the proposals that were made to this government by the prairie ministers when they were here last Thursday. There is a great deal of talk by this government about participatory democracy. One way of course is to involve the other levels of government, to involve the provinces. I submit that to let those ministers come down here and have those discussions on Friday, to come to whatever understanding they may have come to, then to throw it out the window and say "it is all off; we are going to put this bill through" is certainly not carrying out participatory democracy.
People are becoming somewhat discouraged about what is going on. I hear people who are on the other side of the fence say on the radio that they are disturbed because the debate is going on and there is obstructionism by the opposition. They ask us why we do not let the government get its way. The other side of the picture is that the government has a responsibility to the people of this country, the responsibility to keep its word. I submit that that is not being done by holding this debate this week, and I submit that the government is not measuring up to its responsibility to maintain the law by its failure to pay the amounts specified under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. I see that Your Honour is on the edge of the chair, so I will sit down. On the stabilization bill side, the amount that would go to the farmer depends upon the total sales situation for the year. If we are comparing payments which may go to farmers, we have to be honest enough to recognize that that contingency is a very large one. Although the treasury will make a specific payment of $35 million in certains years, the contingent liability under Bill C-244 is unlimited. As I say, under the bill it is unlimited. It is not my attitude, but that of the hon. member for Edmonton West who raised the question. We have never raised it in the House. We are demanding the introduction of a comprehensive farming policy in Canada equally favourable to eastern and western farmers. That's what we want! I think everyone is aware of our position on this subject. Unfortunately, for years, considerable time has been spent in stirring up the West against the East and vice versa by saying: If things are going wrong out West, it is because Ottawa is giving too much money to the East; and if they are going badly in the East, it is because Ottawa is giving too much to the West. People and regions are being raised against each other by the introduction of bills like this one, Bill C-244, or by taking incoherent positions like the ones we see here in this House.
Mr. Speaker, what do we mean by a global policy? The farmers from the west, no more than those from the east, would come begging to the federal government if they were sure they could sell their products. Had western farmers been sure they could sell their wheat at a profit, Bill C-244 would not be before the House. The same goes for eastern farmers, whether it be in the dairy industry or general agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, that is what is lacking-certainty. Were a bill to be introduced to guarantee markets for the whole Canadian agricultural industry, were the government to take the required steps to store that production, the problem would be solved.
Two years ago, we had a surfeit of wheat. Next year, there may be a shortage, not because of a crop failure, but because, at one point, we found an export market for it. The situation is the same in all fields of production in Canada. And I hold the government responsible for that state of affairs. I maintain that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has not been a good salesman, that he did not find the necessary markets where our surpluses in Canada could be exported.
Instead of travelling to Australia, New Zealand or other countries of the world, he should be investigating export possibilities for our products. And we, members of Parliament pass a law to guarantee western and eastern farmers alike the sale of their entire production. This would be a permanent solution to the problem which is raised every year by the opposition, the government or the various farmer associations across Canada.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-244 has given rise to controversy, as every body has noticed, especially among farmers. I receive letters from socialist areas of Saskatchewan, from
southern Alberta, asking that the bill not be passed. People from Medicine Hat for example urge that the government not be allowed to change its present policy, namely the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. Farmers are utterly confused. Why? Because some believe that the government is interfering in the management of their business or seeking to take hold of their properties or to deprive them of their freedom, while others think that the government wants to assist them.
Here in this House we have just been listening to 45 minutes of idle discussions. Hon. members have talked about $38 million, $30 million, $20 million, $113 million, $170 million. Proposals range from paying farmers to filling the deficit of the wheat pool or making payments to another organization. We no longer know where we are heading.
Mr. Speaker, there is something which I believe would be wise to do. That would be to stop using farmers as political feelers, particularly in western Canada. This theme has been exceedingly exploited for years. I see the minister nodding in the affirmative, but a former liberal leader, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, also used farmers for political ends. I saw progressive conservatives like John Bracken of Manitoba using also the western farmers for their political maneuvers. Besides, they have succeeded in raising the west against the east in Canada and vice versa while everywhere in the country farmers are faced with the same problem. In fact, all the classes of our society are fighting these same difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, let us stop playing politics with that. For a month now farmers have been saying: Take a decision; come to any kind of agreement. The government persists in refusing to avail itself of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and says: All that is included in Bill C-244; it allows the $100 million grant. Some people want to dissect this bill-to take the $100 million out in order to give them to the farmers and leave consideration of the problems for later.
The government stubbornly refuses to change its stand while, farmers are kept waiting and have to borrow money from finance companies and pay extravagant interest rates. One can imagine their dissatisfaction, not only with the government but also with this House, which just gets lost in useless debate.
Mr. Speaker, time has come for us to make a decision. If some oppose the bill, let them vote against it. If some are in favour of the bill, let them vote accordingly. But let us come to a vote on this bill. I am aware that the government can make use of Standing Orders 75A, 75B and 75C and demand that a vote be taken, but time has come for us to do so anyway. In any event, a vote will eventually be called on this bill-and we will realize, as usual, that the government has a majority. Thus we will not be accused of having harmed the farmers of western Canada or of eastern Canada. It seems to me it is time we assume our responsibilities and take the vote. Let those who are against the bill vote that way and let those who are in favour prove it. We will see the result and I hope it will be in the best interests of western farmers and especially of the wheat producers of western Canada.

speechtext:
I would like to say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that I view Bill C-244 as a typical example of a government not really knowing what western Canada wants or needs, so doing the next best thing, in their view, and placing before the farmers of western Canada a bill loaded with what I believe to be the true Liberal philosophy of supply management and government control. If one views Bill C-244, along with Bill C-176 which we were lately discussing, it makes a person stop and ask himself just how far is a government willing to go before it openly advocates complete government control of our industry.
In the past few weeks, as a practical farmer and as a member for a rural constituency, I have had many conversations with farmers and it is quite apparent that many farmers are very sceptical of the grain stabilization bill. This has come about for a number of reasons, one of them being that when their farm organization representatives came to Ottawa to appear before the committee, very few of recommendations made by the farm organizations were adopted or, for that matter, very seriously thought about by the minister responsible for the Wheat Board. Some of the recommendations to which I refer were:
1.	A reduction in farmers' contributions to the plan and a more rightful, responsive position taken by the government;
2.	The transitional payment to be paid out immediately and then the legislation discussed for its long term effects;
3.	That the federal government share the costs of carrying the necessary reserve stocks of grain by paying carrying charges annually on approximately 400 million bushels of all grain;
4.	An inflation factor to be built into the legislation; and
5.	Losses in the grain pool accounts not to be paid out of the stabilization fund.
One has to look very carefully and be somewhat sceptical of just where the government is going and what it is trying to do as far as western agriculture is concerned. It has been said many times by both opposition parties as well as by witnesses present at the committee proceedings that if the bill were not improved the initial impact of the legislation would likely, for a period of time, result in the reduction of the level of income available to the producer because of the reduction of the levy and the termination of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. Moreover, the protection' afforded the level of farm income will be altogether inadequate over a given period of time.
Regardless of what may be said, Mr. Speaker, I believe that Bill C-244 is a vehicle designed to enable the federal government to bring to a conclusion the number of federal policies which relate to the expenditure of public funds for the support of agriculture and, I might add, without compensating the prairie farmers on a comparable basis. As an example of this, I would draw attention to the government ending its commitment to guarantee initial prices for wheat, oats and barley under Clause 15. In 1968-69, this guarantee for wheat resulted in payment by the government of approximately $17 million to the Canadian Wheat Board. Operating losses under the grain stabilization bill would not be charged against the fund to which the farmer is contributing a share of the money which is to constitute the fund. I would also refer to the ending of government support of storage payments under
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act for wheat in commercial storage, 178 million bushels under the terms of clause 33.
It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that payment by the government for the carrying of a reasonable inventory of grains to meet world trade requirements is still a valid philosophy of agricultural policy, although this could be done other than through the existing Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. This Act has, since its inception 15 years ago, paid out an annual average of $40 million. The total burden of commercial storage will now fall upon the grain producers. Reference has also been made to the repealing of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act under which the federal payments have averaged $6 million annually since 1939. Discontinuance of the policy requiring millers to purchase wheat entering the domestic market for human consumption at a basic rate of $1.95 j will result in an annual loss of some $12 million to $15 million dollars to wheat producers at present price levels without a compensating payment or reduction in prices.
The commitment of the government to the program under Bill C-244 will, I believe, be roughly $40 million. The proposals in Bill C-244 essentially aim at stabilizing the income from grains relative to current conditions. As any farmer from western Canada will tell you, stabilizing incomes relevant to current conditions is just not good enough. Conditions in a good many areas of western Canada are very serious indeed. Farmers have gone through a winter where there was a terrific cash shortage; they have gone through the spring in which there was a cash shortage and now they face the prospect of no additional government help, simply because the government will not pay them the money that is rightly owing to them under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act.
The provisions of this bill for stability relative to this situation are unattractive. Were we heading into a period of deflation we could, of course, view the proposals in a different light. We are, however, inclined to the view that inflation will continue more or less along the pattern of recent times. Should this turn out to be the case, then the stabilization plan, as proposed by the government, seems entrely inadequate. Farmers are in the poorest segment of the Canadian economy, with the exception of old age pensioners and others on limited and fixed incomes, to absorb the current effects of inflation. A farmer's essential expenses, such as taxes and cost of living, are related to the domestic economy. On the other hand, export sales are locked into a situation which involves virtually no bargaining, in a market which is further depressed by competition, in many cases from government-subsidized stocks. In addition, farmers have absolutely no influence over trade arrangements and credit programs which may be unfavourable to them. In these circumstances, the effects of inflation are such that the income accruing to producers of grain for export faces continued erosion. Should the inflation rate be as low as even 4 per cent per year, it is not difficult to calculate the disastrous position in which grains producers will find themselves five or six years from now. And I contend the bill before us will do absolutely nothing against the inflation of which I have been speaking.
I have heard the minister say that if any constructive criticism were voiced in this debate he would be willing to

Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
listen. However, after seeing what happened during the weekend I find some difficulty in believing this statement. I suppose constructive criticism has a different meaning for different people, but I should like to add two or three points which in my view would make the legislation more palatable.
First of all, I think there must be more direct producer representation on the grain stabilization board itself. These producers must have some real influence at the decision making level. Second, I believe there must be some means, as I have said before, whereby we can build into the plan a cost of living or inflation index. I do not believe that this is an unreasonable request to make. Third, I think the money that is rightly owing under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act must be paid out to the farmers and the act updated. I believe these demands are not unreasonable. If these points are not given any consideration in any form whatsoever then of necessity I feel I must vote against the legislation when the vote is finally called.
In closing, I should like to add that in dealing with a total policy package with respect to income protection for the western grain growers we must contemplate an adequate two-price system for their products. This was again mentioned this afternoon. It is just not right that Canada should be virtually the only wheat producing nation that accepts world price levels as an adequate guide to prices that should fairly be paid in the marketplace by domestic consumers. A look at the statistics indicates the shocking fact that since World War II there has been essentially no increase in grain prices, which means no increase in the amount farmers receive for flour and cereal products sold to the consumers of this country. I believe this situation must be corrected by substantially increasing the price received by the farmers for grain used for domestic human consumption. The impact of this increase on the consumer would be very small, since the great bulk of the cost of cereal products purchased by the consumers consists of transportation, processing and distribution charges.
We are debating this piece of legislation today because it leaves a great deal to be desired so far as a grain stabilization policy for western Canada is concerned. In addition, the government has ignored the pleas of groups that represent farmers. We must draw on someone for expert advice and these groups made an attempt this spring to present their case in Ottawa. But the fact is that the government has ignored their pleas, just as it has ignored the recommendations of the agricultural committee of the House of Commons, and this indicates that the government is bent upon putting through this legislation whether or not it be beneficial to the farming community. The government does not want to hear the other side of the argument.
Once again may I say I will not be able to vote for the legislation in its present form because I sincerely believe it will not produce a proper grain stabilization policy for western farmers.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the debate on this amendment, I want to make it

very clear at the beginning that if there is any question in the minds of hon. members that we are not going to try to hold up the bill, then I suggest that that is exactly our intention at the present time. There is no question at all that somewhere along the line the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and the real issue in the debate on the stabilization plan have got lost. There is no question whatever that the government is now trying to blackmail the western producers into thinking that they have two choices, either to accept the payment under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act or to accept the mythical $100 million that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) held out on his telecast the other night.
The Temporary Wheat Reserves Act is not the real issue here; the real issue is whether the stabilization plan itself is going to be of benefit to the western producers. I am sure the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is convinced that the plan now before the House is not really in the best interests of agricultural producers.
As we witness the changing moods in this House of Commons, it is not difficult to realize that proposals are being made for certain reasons that are not compatible with the basic philosophy of the plan. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson) talked this afternoon about the big bonanza that would result from the payment of $100 million. Not too long ago, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool published a bulletin which indicated that the average payment would be about $560 on the maximum quota of 640 acres. I suggest that this payment is a carrot being held out by the minister in order to get the bill through this House, a bad bill to say the least. The minister is wrong if he thinks he can get the bill through the House in its present form, no matter what kind of blackmail is used.
We have all heard the saying, which is probably quite true, that the politics of corruption is the misuse of our fellow man. I can think of no greater misuse of our fellow man than what happened in Ottawa over the weekend when the three prairie ministers of agriculture met with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board to discuss the very issue we are debating here at the present time, namely the net incomes of agricultural producers. The whole basis of the amendment before the House is net income; in other words, the exact amount the agricultural producers will receive.
Instead of the minister being forthright and telling the agriculture ministers of the three prairie provinces that he really was not concerned about the incomes of prairie producers, he told the press something else. While I was in Moose Jaw the Moose Jaw Times-Herald carried the headline "Government to delay debate on bill", and the first paragraph of the article was as follows:
The federal government has agreed not to proceed with its prairie grain stabilization bill for at least another week to allow provincial governments, farmers and others to consider its implications "and its relationship to over-all income of grain producers."
To my knowledge, the three prairie Ministers of Agriculture came to Ottawa in order to discuss the very issues we are debating today, and which we will be debating in this House for many more days. Even though the minister in charge of the Wheat Board may have wanted to delay the bill for a week to try to bargain on some of
October 5, 1971

the provisions in the bill, he was probably not allowed that delay by the Prime Minister and the cabinet generally. It seems strange indeed that when the western provinces would like to have some dialogue with a government that is responsible for the agricultural economy they should be betrayed. They have been double-crossed, and they learned about this double-cross only when they returned home.
I have referred to the saying that the politics of corruption is the misuse of our fellow man, and this government stands condemned on every count of misusing the agricultural producers of this country. When I was in Moose Jaw over the weekend, I talked to several farmers about this bill and asked them what they would do if they were members of the House. There was no question in their minds that they did not want this stabilization plan in its present form.
We have all heard much debate in this House during the last few weeks about the government breaking the law, and this will be decided by a court. The real issue is that the government is responsible for the plan it would like to bring in, and members of the opposition are responsible for seeing that the plan suits the best interests of the agricultural economy. Every member of the opposition, as well as the independent members in the House, should decide whether or not this stabilization plan deals with the net income of farmers today. It is in this regard our amendment was proposed. It clarifies the bill in that it designates a time period and spells out in clear terms exactly what the legislation is intended to do.
Not long ago I asked the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) the following question dealing with this subject:
Can the minister say if, under the proposal for a prairie grain stabilization plan, any final report has been prepared on the consolidation of small farm units into units of more efficient size? If so, can the minister say whether this report will be made available to the House?
The minister said in answer:
Mr. Speaker, the paragraph in the statement to which the hon. member refers had reference to some plans being developed by my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture. Further details about these plans were subsequently issued by the minister, and I know that a full copy was distributed to all hon. members of the House.
I suggest that the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board misled the House when he said these plans were distributed to all members. In an attempt to find out whether I had misplaced my copy I found that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) had in fact distributed copies in certain communities in order that people there could consider the proposals, but the plan was not widely distributed. This further compounds the situation, because the statement that all members received a copy is not true.
The same thing applies to the suggestion that the minister was prepared to meet the ministers of agriculture and delay, possibly for one week, the discussion of this bill. We find that is untrue. This is the situation in which we find ourselves, yet we hear the suggestion that we are using the farmers as pawns in this game. People dedicated to the principle of equality for .all in this country, particularly
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
those in the agricultural sector, realize that the bill before us does not meet the necessary criteria. I sincerely hope that no member of the House will take for granted that it does. The issue hinges on the net income feature and the amendment before us is directed toward that point.
When I asked about plans to adjust farm units to a more efficient size there was no answer. Just as in this case, the farmers know nothing about the plan where it refers to adjustment of farm units. How can we in this House make an intelligent decision as to whether the stabilization plan is in the best interests of our nation when we are not told specifically what the government has in mind? Municipalities and small agricultural communities must depend on net income and the return to agricultural producers. They must also become familiar with the precise intent of this bill before any sensible decision can be made. It seems strange that the government has refused to supply these details.
We in this party realize that there must be collective bargaining and we firmly believe that in the interests of the agricultural sector of our economy there must be a cooling-off period in that collective bargaining. Our newspapers referred to this during the weekend, but we now find there is to be no cooling-off period. The minister is adamant, as is the Prime Minister, that anything he thinks is good for the farm should be accepted by everyone. When we consider the situation we realize that what he thinks is good for the farm is not good in any way, shape or form.
Questions were asked earlier today about an advertisement which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post. It also appeared in the most recent edition of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. It related to net income, and I am wondering whether the farmer is being charged for this type of propaganda which appears in the newspapers. In the August edition of Saturday Night magazine I find an advertisement under the heading, "Prairie farmers gear production to world demand". It states that it was issued under the authority of the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture, and reads in part:
The government of Canada is helping this development with its new prairie grain policy-providing "package" programs for all grains, encouraging increased pasture, setting up a new quota system, providing a stabilization program to offset poor years and making sure the farmer gets advance information on world grain conditions at planting time.
I wonder whether the cost of this propaganda is being deducted from the receipts of western farmers. Who is behind this kind of propaganda, and is the cost being deducted from farmers' incomes? The cost of this type of advertisement must be tremendous, because we all know that the cost of a full-page, coloured ad in a newspaper is high. We do not know that there is any justification for this kind of thing, but we know that one of these advertisements was authorized by the Keep the Stabilization Plan Committee. This reminds me of the KOD plan of a few years ago in Saskatchewan. It was the Keep Our Doctors plan. Perhaps the same people are involved in this propaganda. If this type of propaganda is to continue, then the people should be given a clear explanation of the stabilization plan. The name is peculiar in itself because there is no stabilization plan as yet. These advertisements

We have a minister responsible for the Wheat Board and for immigration and manpower who is also the minister who has suggested the Local Opportunities program, as they call the new program for this winter, which they are afraid to start too early because the snow might not fly for another two weeks or so. This minister is responsible for all these areas. How could he possibly be thoroughly familiar and conversant with the area affecting the income of the agricultural producer?
It would seem to me that if the Prime Minister wanted to perform a real service to this country he would divide the portfolio of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Hum-boldt. He ought to look into the situation and place somebody else in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. This stabilization plan, involving the net income of the farmer, is a full-time, on-the-ground process. How can any minister be conversant with the problems of each and every department he has been given an interest in and supervision of?
It would seem to me that the agricultural producer in this country has been shortchanged by the Liberal government and the Prime Minister when a minister is not put completely in charge of the agricultural economy. We have a minister of agriculture from the west and a minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, also from the west. I think each looks to the other and wonders what jurisdiction each has. In the end, damn little is done for the agricultural economy. We hear much about the number of people who are urging that we adopt the stabilization plan in order to get this so-called $100 million. However, we should consider the people who are still opposed to it. An advertisement in a Regina paper tried to associate the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool with it, and yesterday the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool made very clear that they are not associated with the advertisement.

If we are going to be serious about

The subamendment was moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). It amended the amendment moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave). As I said before, it goes to the very core of the issue that we are discussing today and have discussed for the past few days in the House. The amendment and the subamendment deal essentially with a new formula which would make the stabilization plan one that could be accepted by western farmers and western farm organizations.
It seems to me very strange that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) will not listen to some of the suggestions that come from this side of the House. We do not pretend to be experts, to know it all, to have all the answers to the farm problems. We are not like the minister in that respect. But one thing we do know is that farm organizations and farmers themselves are not very happy with the bill that is before us. For that reason we are doing all we can to change the bill and to make it more acceptable to the farmers.
I suggest to the minister that we will continue as long as we can and as emphatically as we can to convince him that he should change the bill which he presented to the House. This past summer when I was out in my constit-

uency I had the opportunity to speak with literally hundreds of farmers. One of their main concerns was with the stabilization bill, the way it was drafted and the formula that would be applied to them if it passed the House.
These farmers are not letting us pull the wool over their eyes. They know what is happening. They knew what was happening in the provincial election when they studied the stabilization bill. The results of that election are indicative of what they thought of some of the proposals in the stabilization bill. It is very significant, as I and many of my colleagues have said, that all the major farm organizations are unanimous in their opposition to the bill before us, organizations such as the wheat pools of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, the Federation of Agriculture, the Farmers Union and the United Grain Growers. All the main organizations and farm spokesmen are unanimous in saying that this bill is not good enough and that it must be changed if it is to help meaningfully farmers in the western provinces.
We have the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta which differ in their ideology and in their interpretation of the policies that should be presented to their people. But despite that they are unanimous in their conclusion that this bill will not help the farmers. The ministers of these provinces came to Ottawa last Friday to meet with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. They presented to him in a very sincere and serious way some alternatives which he should consider for changing the regulations and some of the main features of this bill. It is our understanding that as a result of that meeting the minister agreed to consider most seriously some of these recommendations which would change the bill and take into account costs of production, net income, and other matters.
Then suddenly we find that although a moratorium of one week was promised we are discussing Bill C-244 once again. Did the minister double-cross the ministers of agriculture of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta; and, if so, why did he do this? Perhaps we are too harsh with the minister. We are calling him all sorts of names. I think the minister sincerely wanted to consider some of these changes, but he went to the Prime Minister's office and was told, "No, thou shalt not do this, Otto", and Otto had to come back here and reintroduce the bill yesterday afternoon. I think that is the story. The minister probably tried. Perhaps the minister says different things in cabinet meetings than he does in the House, but the Prime Minister runs this country with an iron fist, in a unilateral and autocratic way.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I am very glad that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board said what he did. It seems to me that he is telling the truth but he insinuates that the provincial ministers of agriculture might not have told the truth when they said they had an agreement with him that he would go back and consider the proposal to have a moratorium of one week. Were the three ministers of agriculture not telling the truth? I hope the minister in charge of the Wheat Board will at least have enough common courtesy to trust the ministers of agriculture of the three prairie provinces.
I am amazed that the minister would not listen to the ministers of agriculture of the prairie provinces, that he would show such lack of sensitivity toward the western farmers whom he is supposed to represent. I was sure he would at least consider their recommendations and would not double-cross them by bringing this bill back suddenly as he has done. Perhaps the decision was not taken in the Prime Minister's office. If it was not, I am very surprised that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board would take the responsibility on his own shoulders. I am sure farmers in my constituency and all across the Prairies will be very interested to know that the minister himself unilaterally made this decision and not the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I have said all along that the farm organizations do not want this bill. We should listen to them and do some of the things they suggest. Do we not do this because we are afraid of the farmers, afraid of their ideas and of letting them participate? All we are asking on this side of the House is that we have a stabilization bill which is acceptable to the farmers of this country.
Earlier today the minister said that perhaps the figures used by the Prime Minister in his telecast on Sunday night were not correct. I think all of us listened to the Prime Minister. I have before me the transcript of what he said. He was talking about the $112 million that will be given to the farmers under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act if it remains in effect. To set the record straight, I should like to quote a short excerpt from his remark as follows:
Let's first compare them in terms of money. For the last crop year, under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, we would be in process of paying the western farmer $62 million, for the crop year which we are now in, we would probably have to pay him some time next year something like $30 million, and for the crop year after that $20 million, for a total of $112 million.
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
These are the figures used by the Prime Minister, the figures which the minister in charge of the Wheat Board tried to change today. I think the minister should consult more closely with the Prime Minister's office, because the Prime Minister will probably want to change some of the things the minister has been saying to us.
The amendments before us are crucial to this bill. The government should listen and accept them. If they would accept these amendments and bring the costs of production and the net income of farmers into consideration, then I am sure that members of the opposition would be more favourably impressed by the bill and would consider giving it speedy passage. If the minister is at all sincere, then we can send the $100 million out to the farmers immediately, as was suggested today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). We could then study the stabilization bill more closely, listen to the farm organizations and perhaps iron out some of the things that they do not like.
Some members who have participated in this debate are familiar with an advertisement which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post protesting against some opposition members speaking against the stabilization bill. The advertisement states that the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has now joined the government in approving this bill. But I think he would like us to make it clear that this is not the case, that it is misleading advertising and that he is not in favour of the bill. The wheat pool speaks for tens of thousands of farmers in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool radio report of September 29 began as follows:
With all the opposition to the proposed grain receipts and income stabilization plan, it's time government took a fresh look at its proposals.
Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and other farm organizations have suggested a number of changes to the plan because it does little to improve the individual farmer's net income. They have pointed out that income would be stabilized at too low a level.
That can hardly be interpreted as support for the stabilization bill, and it is a very good indication of where the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool stands. I could go on and on reading press statements of the Alberta Wheat Pool, the Manitoba Wheat Pool and other farm organizations, all of them saying that the bill before us is not good enough and asking that changes be introduced immediately.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board, and the Prime Minister, have said that we have a choice between A and B-the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and the stabilization bill. I am sure that anyone who thinks at all knows that this is not the case. It is not so clear. First of all, we cannot just consider the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. The PFAA, for example, will disappear if we pass the bill before us.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, a good argument could be made to show that the farmers will not receive $170 million, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested, but only $65 million over the next two years. That is the picture if one considers only the short-term aspects of the bill.
Another matter concerning many of my constituents and people throughout our farming community is the

October 5, 1971
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
long-term ramifications of Bill C-244. The figure of $35 million was used by the Prime Minister on Sunday evening in this telecast. This figure, which is supposed to be paid out of the federal treasury each year, was based on total receipts of $900 million in the grains industry. Four per cent of that figure is $35 million. Let me remind hon. members that in many years less than $900 million worth of grain will be sold. In some years we may sell only $700 million or $800 million worth which means that only $28 million or $32 million per year will be contributed from the federal treasury to farmers over the long term. That is to say, over the long term the farmer who gets this money will be no better off. He might only get about $28 million, $32 million or $35 million from the federal treasury every year.Those amounts will apply only to farmers who will be getting benefits from the stabilization fund.
Many of my colleagues and some farm organizations have pointed out that not all farmers will necessarily benefit from the fund as it is presently constituted. Many parts of the plan and some of the regulations to be brought in may prevent a farmer receiving benefits from the fund unless the bill is amended. Therefore, in the long term the fund will not help the farmer and it will not stabilize farm income. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, at best the plan will be but an insurance policy. If there happens to be a disastrous year, it will insure a certain proportion of income received by the grain farmer.
Many other things have been said about the fund. Arguments have been put forward as to why we should very seriously consider the amendments which are before the House. Hon. members have pointed out that the bill does not take into account the real costs of production. Why should the farmer have to bear the brunt of increased production costs? Why should farmers have to subsidize food stores or the consumer part of our economy? Why should not a farmer at least be paid an increasing amount, so that he can keep up with increases in production costs?
The minister said yesterday that you could not include in a stabilization bill a clause to take into consideration costs of production. I submit that you could easily do that. It has been done in other government plans. I am sure that an economist could easily work out such a provision which could be incorporated in the bill we are discussing. Why do we not listen to farmers and farm organizations and introduce into this bill or a bill like it a two-price system for grain? That would help, in a genuine and immediate way, the farmers of western Canada, particularly those in the middle and lower income brackets.
There is another long-term consideration we ought to take into account when debating this bill. If the bill passes it will stabilize farm incomes at a very low level. According to people who know more about this subject than most members of the House, this bill will be the first step toward implementing the recommendations of the task force on agriculture. Those task force recommendations seek to expedite the exodus of people from rural Canada to urban centres. Really we are talking about a whole life style which is being threatened by the provisions of the bill. We are talking about the culture of our rural society. Why do we continue pushing people from the small centres and farms into the large, unplanned cities? These are matters we ought to consider and deal with in a bill of this

sort. It is only natural that we should consider these issues. They should be top priorities, and not the priorities the minister seems to have given them.
I say as sincerely as I can that the minister ought to consider accepting some of the recommendations of the three prairie ministers of agriculture. The minister should again look at the briefs of the wheat pools of the provinces, at the briefs presented by the Farmers Union and the Federation of Agriculture and adopt some of the amendments they suggest. That would not cost very much and would be fair to the farmer. That is all I am asking. Let us bring in a bill that the farmer wants and from which he will benefit.

We will not give the minister the credit for negotiating directly with the parties, because Parliament will make the ultimate decision.
Certain alleged facts have been discussed this afternoon. I am sure that most hon. members would agree that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) did not tell the entire story in respect of the figures he used. The farmers of western Canada are not the least bit confused by the situation. They are living from day to day. They know how much income they enjoy and where that income comes from.
As has been made clear, the subamendment before the House seeks to apply the stabilization bill to a grain farmer's net income rather than to his gross income. The farmers of western Canada know what goes into gross income. They know that this year they grew a bumper crop of between 1.25 billion and 1.5 billion bushels of wheat. The western farmer also knows that under normal conditions a crop this size means that he will get considerably more money than he would in years of lesser production. Two or three years ago the farmer was talking about $2 per bushel of wheat; he was anticipating that No. 1 Northern would fetch $2 per bushel. The Liberal party promised a two-price system as well as $2 plus per bushel. The farmer found that prices were around $1.76 a bushel. Now, Mr. Speaker, with a bumper crop the farmer is getting $1.42.

speechtext:
That is shocking.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS TO WESTERN CANADA PRODUCERS IN YEARS WHEN RECEIPTS BELOW FIVE-YEAR AVERAGE
speechtext: It is sad that farmers' costs did not go down at all. It costs just as much to fertilize an acre of wheat land in western Canada-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS TO WESTERN CANADA PRODUCERS IN YEARS WHEN RECEIPTS BELOW FIVE-YEAR AVERAGE
speechtext: It costs more under Liberal inflation.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS TO WESTERN CANADA PRODUCERS IN YEARS WHEN RECEIPTS BELOW FIVE-YEAR AVERAGE
speechtext:
Yes. As the hon. member points out, under inflation everything costs more. Every year the increase is 4, 5 or 6 per cent. At any rate, the farmer puts on the same amount of fertilizer, at a higher cost. He drives a tractor which uses as much gasoline or kerosene as before, but gasoline and kerosene cost more. The farmer uses the same number of hired men, at higher wages. He must borrow more money now to operate his farm and pay considerably more interest on it than before.
All the factors that go into production costs have increased. At the same time, the farmer is getting less for his produce than before. The more he produces, the less he gets. I think it is a fact that the farmers break-even point is considerably higher than even the gross income that he is receiving. Hence, the farmer is in a deficit position now. The higher prices go, the worse his position will become. This bill does not take that factor into consideration at all.
Some time ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) set up a task force on agriculture. There have been two major agricultural meetings in Canada. Several major recommendations were made to the government. One was that the government stabilize the income of western farmers. This, of course, is where the government got the crackpot notion that eventually evolved into this ludicrous bill. It is supposed to give the farmer something but it will take away more than it gives. There are other factors.
The minister spoke about the right of the government to refuse to make payments under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. We were told in committee that the costs of storing over 180 million bushels of grain in a crop year were to be paid to the farmer at the rate of seven, eight or nine cents a bushel. Unless the system of storage in elevators, the method of handling grain in the terminals and the transit and loading systems are changed, you are not likely to get away from the fact there has to be in storage the production of one or two crop years. That production can be stored in a number of places.
A few minutes ago my colleague very eloquently pointed out that it is time the government made up its mind about what it intends to do with regard to storage. Other countries have done this. The government will have to develop a grain supply bank in Canada to meet our commitments. This must be for an extended period of time, at least three years. The government, the country and the economy are interrelated in the production of western grains. If we do not keep a large enough supply on hand to meet our commitments in case there is a disaster in an area of grain production, we will not keep up with what is a normal pattern in other countries.
Governments of other countries are responsible for the sale and storage of food. This relieves the farmer of storage costs. To say that the Wheat Board is responsible for the costs, and the final payment to the farmer is the selling price less the costs, obviously puts all the costs

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this amendment partly because I wish to comment on the figures given by the minister as to the amount of money that would be owing under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act versus Bill C-244. The minister stated that there is $62.1 million owing already, with $30.8 million likely, and an estimated $20 million for the present crop year. But the minister stated that only $38.6 million will reach the farmers out of the $62.1 million. He implied that the balance, $23.5 million, would not reach the farmers and would not be used.
I should like to point out that this money goes to the Wheat Board to be used in its operations in taking care of pools which have been in deficit, and under the new act, when a pool is in trouble it will be paid a sum out of the stabilization fund to help them with carrying charges, and so on, related to grain in storage. Almost certainly, if this bill should pass in its present form there will have to be an increase in the handling charges of grain, so the farmers will have to make further payments out of the proceeds from their grain in order to make up what was the government's obligation under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act.
Although the farmers may not necessarily receive the exact amount of their payments into the pools under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, still it goes to their benefit because it is used to help carry the Wheat Board so that it can provide the service of marketing the grain. The minister stated that with the $100 million that would be paid under Bill C-244, the farmer would be a lot better off. This is not necessarily so, because he included an estimated $17.5 million for the next two years that would be paid
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
out of the farmers' pockets, to be matched by $35 million each year from the government. This, however, will go into the stabilization fund and there will not be any immediate benefit to the farmer unless there should be a disastrous crop failure.
The effect of this legislation, really, is that the government will not be paying out any substantial amount of money in the next five years. Unless there should be a tremendous disaster, it will not have to pay out any money. So at a time when things are extremely bad the government is able to wash itself of the farm industry for the next five years. What about the prospects for this year, which the minister attempted to say are extremely good? In the Richardson grain letter of September 30 we find these comments:
Reports from around the world paint a rather gloomy picture for the Canadian producer. According to the Canadian commercial officer in New Delhi, India is becoming self-sufficient in wheat. They have already acquired the 5 million tons buffer stock of imported wheat, and the Food Corporation's target of buying four million tons from local farmers has already been exceeded by one million tons. Supplies are still flowing in steadily, leading to what is being currently referred to as "the problem of plenty". India may not require imports and could well be seeking export markets next year. Some are even so optimistic as to maintain that India's wheat revolution has come to stay to an extent that future poor monsoons will not have any significant effect on production and supplies.
The United Kingdom harvest is expected to be at an all-time high; the EEC countries harvested record crops and the U.S. feed grains production, which includes corn, oats, barley and sorghum, is expected to total 198 million tons, 24 per cent more than last year, and all-wheat production at 1,625 million bushels is a record high. The deficiency countries are mainly in North Africa and the Middle East where we were expected to sell a lot of barley, for one thing, but the Commodity Credit Corporation-an arm of the U.S. department of agriculture-has started to sell barley-
-at a very low price. Referring to oilseeds, the worldwide burdensome supplies of flax are well known and this holds out very little promise for any advance in price. In rapeseed, European supplies are estimated to be 120,000 metric tons more than last year, and with the increase in our own crop of around 30 million bushels we have substantial rapeseed on hand. So hon. members can see that this bill comes at a crucial time for western agriculture.
What are the main problems connected with this bill? I would like to enumerate them as I see them. The fact is that it comes at a time when there have been four years of poor income and only one good year. This gives a very low average on which to base the formula for crop payments. Five years ago it amounted to approximately $1,400 million, but in the last four years it has been between $800 million to $900 million to $1 billion. So in view of the crop expectations, the government will not have to pay out much money from the fund in the next five years, and almost certainly nothing in the next two years. Nevertheless, farmers will be paying 2 per cent of their gross income at a time when they can ill afford it.
What can be done? I suggest that the minister should reduce the farmers' contributions in the next two years to nothing, or at the most to 1 per cent for at least the next five years. After the plan has been in force for five years the amount could be increased to 2 per cent if conditions warrant it. However, at this time to impose a 2 per cent

levy is not in the interest of the farmers. Furthermore, for the next two years there should be some base, regardless of what the average is, below which farm income should not be allowed to fall. What about payments under the bill? Little thought was given to the type of payment that would have to be made. Agriculture is not a monolithic industry. It is not made up of two, three, four or even ten large companies. It is made up of 200,000 grain producers who live in a large area 400 miles wide by 1,000 or more miles long, people who experience different conditions and whose districts are entirely different.
The fact that payments will not be made for the whole of the designated area below the previous five years' average means that great hardship will result. Of these 200,000 farmers, at any one time and in any one year- even in the best years-10,000 to 20,000 will be in difficulties. They may easily find themselves in serious trouble through no fault of their own, while their neighbours might be enjoying the best financial years of their lives. What will happen if these 10,000 to 20,000 farmers who are in trouble each year have a 2 per cent levy imposed on them in that particular year? What can be done to make this bill more workable?
The least we could do is to make payments to crop districts. At least this would narrow down and help to smooth out some of the injustices. It would prevent discrimination which would take place with this type of pay-out that the government proposes under the bill. Unless something like this is done, the movement of farmers off the land will accelerate and farmers who are in difficulty will be pushed over the edge because they will receive no payment but will in fact have to pay 2 per cent of their meagre gross income in that year. These are some of the comments that I wanted to make on the bill. It is incomprehensible to me that a 2 per cent levy should be applied immediately. It should be reduced to 1 per cent or even to nothing for the first couple of years.
The other point I want to make is that when the program is begun, a different base than the previous five years' average should be established. Finally, the method of payment leaves much to be desired. It is not a good method and I think it could be improved so that a workable solution is found to some of the farm problems.

Right, costs of production. There is no reason why farmers cannot be considered in the same light and come to Parliament to ask that their future be looked upon favourably, in the same way that we look upon the future of industrial workers or any other group that comes to Parliament and says, "We are entitled to some sense of security and some sense of support from the other people in our society".
One thing is certain, Mr. Speaker, that inflation is a fact of life and we will have to live with it. I do not think there is any economist or any person who is analysing the situation in Canada, the United States or any part of the world who will say that there will not be inflation in future. We hope that it will not be a galloping kind of inflation, but we know we will not be able to hold it down to less than 3 per cent.
This means that every single component the farmer uses to produce wheat will rise in price-his truck, his tools, the petrol, the combine, and so on; even the things he needs in order to exist, that he cannot grow himself and requires for sustenance. The very bread that he grows the wheat for will rise in price because of increasing labour costs and the general increase in the cost of living.
This bill says that the farmer will be compensated only if his gross income drops below a certain level. Every year that goes by, his costs of production will increase at a very substantial rate. Even if his income remains steady and the price of wheat remains what it is today, or even if it increases slightly he will lose out on the deal and be caught in the same squeeze that he has been in since the end of the war. The price increases and his gross income do not equate. It is incredible that a bill which claims to seek to stabilize farm income, to give a measure of justice to the farmer and to protect him against the vicissitudes of market hazards, ignores this elementary possibility.
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
The amendment before us is important because it seeks to guarantee the farmer's income by taking costs of production into account. Unless those costs are considered there can be no justice for the farmer on the basis of simply saying, "We will try to maintain your gross income on an average of the last five years". Another bill that was recently before the House also deals with the problem of security. This House passed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which included additional benefits to workers who become unemployed or who cannot work because of ill health. The percentage of the pay which they can draw has been increased. Pregnancy benefits have been allowed under that bill. In fact, what we have done is recognize society's obligations to those who find themselves in difficulty because of technological change or changing market conditions.
Surely the farmer is entitled to the same protection, but this bill does not offer it to him. I think the bill could be drafted to cover it. Acceptance of the subamendment would go a long way toward improving the situation for the farmer. Every year we harvest and sell our wheat, and the next year, if the farmers have done their job in planting it, it grows again. It is renewable, which is not true of oil, gas or minerals. Those resources do not replace themselves. Once they are taken out of the ground, they are lost forever. If we are to pursue an objective in this country, that objective ought to be the export of renewable resources such as wheat and forest products. These are vital commodities and we ought to concentrate on their production.
At present we are undergoing an upheaval. I think we need to develop new trade policies. Our great friends to the south, upon whom the Liberal party from time to time relied when it wanted to get out of trouble, are no longer interested in helping Canadians overcome difficulties caused by our government. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take too much time of the House this evening discussing the amendment to the amendment which is before us. I think we should recall exactly what this subamendment purports to do for the grain economy of western Canada. In my opinion it seeks to deal with a deduction from the gross grain deliveries of farmers in western Canada. This goes to the root of the problem we are facing today and that is why there is in western Canada such fierce opposition to this legislation.
The government seems to be puzzled about why there should be this opposition. In some respects it questions the validity of that opposition. It appears to me, on the basis of mail that crosses my desk, that there is no support for the bill. I have received a significant number of communications-not to be compared with the number I received about Bill C-176-from constituents who definitely oppose this bill. On the other hand, I have received but one letter from a constituent urging passage of the bill. That constituent is a barley grower. He said he did not benefit in any way, shape or form from the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. He thought this was a good opportunity to get some money out of the federal government which, although it was a one-shot deal, was at least something rather than nothing.
I felt it necessary to remind my constituent that he might be paying a rather high price for this one-shot
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
payment, in view of the fact that this legislation proposes what is in my view a new tax on the western grain economy. That is, in this 2 per cent deduction of gross grain deliveries in the foreseeable future there is no real anticipation of ever receiving anything back.
It is useless for the minister to keep reminding us that if this legislation had been in effect since World War II the farmers would have received almost four times the amount of their deductions. We are in a different factual situation. The minister should know that ever since Canada more or less left the International Wheat Agreement by default we have been consistently faced with smaller grain sales abroad. This has been reflected in the radical decline in prairie farm income in t}ie past five years.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of our country. Among other things he is reported to have said that day was the following:
One of the most pressing long-range problems for western farmers is the need for an adequate yearly income to get away from the boom and bust cycle which has become part of prairie farm life. To this end, the Liberals are proposing a plan which in effect, sounds like the equivalent of unemployment insurance for farmers. In good years they would pay into a fund; in bad years they would draw money from the fund, thereby, to a degree, stabilizing their income.
I think most of us would support that concept. So much for the gleam in the eye, so to speak. But when the bill was born it turned out to have some serious abnormalities. One of the most important is that the bill, as contrasted with unemployment insurance, does not apply to individuals. If an individual through no fault of his own becomes unemployed, he needs unemployment assistance. If he has the correct number of stamps on his card and has worked the required number of days, he is eligible for assistance and receives it without equivocation.
The situation is different under this legislation which does not apply to individuals at all but to the average of a group. The hon. member for Palliser ably pointed out that as a result of drought, hail, a grasshopper invasion, even an attack by the Bertha army worms or some other blight peculiar to agriculture on the Prairies, an individual farmer in desperate need of assistance could conceivably be ineligible for assistance under this measure owing to the simple fact that the national average in terms of sales was not sufficiently low to enable him to qualify. Thus, an individual in desperate need of assistance would not get a dime under this measure.
This is a major flaw in the legislation, as pointed out by a number of people. This party and the official opposition feel that the legislation should be based on net rather than gross income. Let me tell the House why I feel this way. I think we are all aware that there are very few sectors of the economy that are stable. For the last 20 years we have experienced a wave of inflation. Stabilizing the income of
Prairie Grain Stabilization Act
farmers sounds fine, but that is only half the problem; you must also stabilize their costs.
Let me give hon. members a revealing example of what has happened to farmers' costs since 1949. These costs have been affected by taxes and interest rates. Using the base 1939 equals 100, by 1949 taxes and interest rates had risen to an index of 149.4. By 1970 that figure had more than doubled, to 323.4. We all know that the farmers need capital. Farms are now large operations; the little halfsections are no longer efficient units and have disappeared. If taxes and interest rates, as one of the indices, have more than doubled during that period, then it appears to me that the income of the farmers would have to match that increase.
The same increase can be shown in the cost of farm machinery. In 1949 the price index had risen to 158.4, and by 1970 had gone up to 339.6. Increases like this are the reason that the members of this party as well as the members of the Conservative party oppose the hill. I submit the cost base of production should be the year 1970. The minister is no longer in the chamber; indeed he is seldom here during the debate. When he is here he rarely listens. He usually just sits in his seat, writes in his notebook and occasionally looks up to give one a baleful stare like a recently hibernated iguana. We are rarely able to reach him.
One needs only to drive across the Prairies to see what is happening to western Canada. It is being depopulated. Small farms are being abandoned in favour of larger units. Opportunities for the people, especially the young, are disappearing. High schools, post offices and drug stores are closing down and whole communities are dispersing. People are migrating to the cities. The same thing is happening in Newfoundland under the present government. The once independent, self-reliant, if not wealthy, people under the new enclosure movement are being chased off the land for economic reasons. Where you once had the land owner you now have millions of Canadians living as cliff-dwelling tenants in cities across Canada, thus creating all kinds of urban problems. It seems to me that if we had done a little more research on rural problems we would have far less need than we have at the moment for a Minister of State for Urban Affairs. Congestion in cities has created many problems for Canadians.
