maintopic: UNITED NATIONS-CANADIAN ACTION TO ACHIEVE REPRESENTATION FOR MAINLAND CHINA AND TAIWAN
UNITED NATIONS-CANADIAN ACTION TO ACHIEVE REPRESENTATION FOR MAINLAND CHINA AND TAIWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 22 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) if the Canadian delegation at the United Nations General Assembly would be making efforts there to bring about a situation whereby the people in Mainland China and Taiwan would be represented in that body by delegates of their de facto governments.
I must say, Sir, that the minister's reply was a good deal more smug than informative. He indicated that there was only one question immediately before the United Nations, and that is who speaks for China, who occupies the China seat; and with a casualness that was somewhat unbecoming he suggested that the question of the future of Taiwan is something for the future to decide.
It sounds so easy and so clever to suggest that there is nothing involved but who occupies the China seat. In fact, Sir, there is a good deal more involved. Involved is the whole concept of universality of membership in the United Nations, a concept in which I believe and in which I thought the present government believed. The support of the Albanian resolution at the General Assembly will mean clearly and definitely the expulsion of the government now in control of affairs in Taiwan. It will mean that over 14 million people will lose representation in what we like to think is a universal body, the United Nations.
I cannot believe that a move which will result in the expulsion of the representative of Taiwan is one which should be entered on so casually and easily by the government of our country. I have long believed that this country should recognize the de facto situation and extend diplomatic recognition to the People's Republic of China, and I am pleased that this has come about although I do not share the view of those who believe that a new era has been entered into by the mere fact of recognition. I am hopeful, however, that it will have a good and helpful effect.
I was especially delighted that the leader of my party made such a valuable and useful visit to Mainland China and made such a good impression there. Indeed, I am not reluctant to say that we should long ago have recognized the de facto situation and extended diplomatic recognition to the government of Peking. But the same pragmatic acceptance of a de facto situation in Mainland China should not be abandoned when we look at Taiwan. The government of Chiang Kai-shek-regardless of what we think of it, and this is not at issue here-undoubtedly is in control and is governing Taiwan just as the government of Mao Tse-tung is governing in Mainland China.
It is easy to use the numbers game and say that the great majority of Chinese citizens are under Mao and that there are only 14 million across the straits. But surely we are not in the game of counting heads, and I think that kind of attitude is unbecoming to a charter member of the United Nations. But if we do count heads, it can be pointed out that there are more people in Taiwan than in two-thirds of the member states of the United Nations
October 5, 1971

today. In other words, Taiwan is not an inconsiderable part of the world community.
Last fall, when the minister announced recognition of Peking by this country, an announcement which was greeted warmly in nearly all quarters of the House, he declared:
Our position ... is that the Canadian government does not consider it appropriate to endorse or to challenge the Chinese government's position on the status of Taiwan.
In other words, the Canadian government took note of Peking's contention in this regard but did not endorse it. It seems to me that in supporting the Albanian resolution at the United Nations the government of Canada would in fact be endorsing the contention of Peking that it, and it alone, speaks for all of China including Taiwan, despite the fact that that island is clearly and obviously administered by a government not subject to Peking. At the very time that the admission of China to the U.N. is being developed, the support of the Albanian resolution would be yielding to the maximum demands of the People's Republic of China in regard to its claims to Taiwan.
Having read the minister's speech, I do not know whether or not Canada will be supporting the Albanian resolution. I do note that at the General Assembly the minister indicated that Canada endorsed the principle of universality and even looked forward to the time when the divided states could be represented at the United Nations. We all say amen to that. But if we move in the direction of admitting the divided states, it would seem inconsistent for us at the same time to adopt a policy which would prevent Taiwan from being represented in the world body.
One cannot but wonder what happened to the eloquently expressed views of the minister's predecessor, the Hon. Paul Martin, who used to win applause from government benches when he said that our policy is not one China or two Chinas but one-China and one-Taiwan. He said in 1967:
We believe Formosa should continue to be a member of that organization and for that reason we will abstain on a resolution which seeks both to seat mainland China and to expel Formosa.
I have noted the present government's casual attitude toward the laws of the land and I am sure they would not at all be inhibited by their own promises; but our recollection is that in the campaign of 1968 it was the Martin one Taiwan, one China policy which was being put forward to the Canadian people as the government's point of view.
I hope, therefore, that it will not be Canada's role to assist in the expulsion of a member from the United Nations, that we will not deny the principle of universality to which we have long given allegiance and that we will not turn our back upon a reasonable, rational settlement of this long troublesome problem of representation in the U.N. for the people of Taiwan and for the people of China.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the question from the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) who sits on the same side of the House as I do, I think it best to reiterate what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) told the House on September 22. This was also in reply to a question by the hon. member for Hillsborough. It is simply that Canada has a one China policy. We consider that the only issue immediately before the United Nations is one of representation, that is, what government should represent the approximately 800 million people living in China.
As hon. members know, although the regime in Taiwan has continued to occupy the Chinese seat in the General Assembly and on the Security Council, a growing number of countries, including Canada, have come to believe that a realistic appreciation of the situation requires that the People's Republic of China be recognized as the government of China and that its representatives should take their place in the Chinese seat at the United Nations.
The issue, therefore, is not one of membership but of who shall represent a country which is already a member, and Canadian policy in the United Nations is consistent with our recognition of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-EFFECT OF AMENDMENTS ON CREDIT UNIONS
INCOME TAX-EFFECT OF AMENDMENTS ON CREDIT UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 9, 1971, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), in the House of Commons, whether he could allay the fears of Canadian credit unions who consider the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act as a threat to their existence. Unfortunately, the Minister of Finance did not have the opportunity to give me a definite reply. That is why I am raising the question this evening.
As an active member of the largest parish credit union in Ontario, the St. Stanislaus Parish Credit Union Limited, with a branch at St. Casimir's parish in the constituency of Parkdale, and as a former member of the board of directors in that credit union 25 years ago, I am familiar with the representations that have been made to the Minister of Finance by Canadian credit unions expressing
8472

October 5, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
their fear of the proposals in clauses 135, 136 and 137 of Bill C-259, an act to amend the Income Tax Act. The whole question of tax reform has been debated by the Canadian public since the publication of the white paper in 1969, and that is very good.
The result, Bill C-259, is now being studied by various people with deep knowledge of the taxation system and its implication for the whole of Canadian life, and they are offering detailed and responsible criticism. I am aware that urgent submissions have been made to the Minister of Finance by representatives of the credit unions from Ontario and other provinces, including the caisses populates in the province of Quebec.
Throughout the history of Canadian tax legislation, credit unions have been treated differently, for tax purposes, from ordinary corporations because they are different in their structure and operation. Credit unions have played a great role in assisting people in lower and middle-income brackets, especially new Canadians in need of loans, to establish themselves in this country, because lending institutions of all descriptions were demanding high securities, high interest rates and other conditions and most of those conditions were, I think, burdensome for most of those people. Consequently, credit unions sprang up and flourished among these groups of people. Credit unions have assisted their members not only with low-cost loans but also with low life insurance premiums and other programs of mutual assistance.
The present income tax amendments affecting credit unions are, to say the least, ambiguous and need clarification. The principle of proper understanding of credit unions and fairness is necessary in devising tax laws with respect to credit unions. A close analysis of the proposed legislation in Bill C-259 reveals that the new taxation will be harmful to the legal characteristics of credit unions and caisses populaires and that these characteristics will place them at a disadvantage with other corporations.
Both the Porter Royal Commission on Banking and the Carter Royal Commission on Taxation recognize the essential "savings nature" of share deposits by a credit union member. Similar recognition should be given in clause 137 of the bill. But the area which causes credit union members the greatest concern is that relating to dividends to members on their share accounts. We have always looked upon these dividends as being an interest payment similar to that paid by chartered banks on their savings accounts. The major difference has been that banks set their rates in advance, whereas credit unions determine their rates on the basis of the profit for the year.
Chartered banks are able to deduct the interest paid on savings accounts from their income to determine their taxable income. The tax reform bill does not appear to provide for the deduction of the dividends paid by credit unions to members on their share accounts. Moreover, there is no provision in the tax reform bill concerning existing allowances for doubtful accounts or the so-called guaranteed fund. The other area which causes a problem concerns the starting point for depreciation of fixed assets.
Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the Minister of Finance to take into consideration the brief presented to him by the National Association of Credit Unions on September 22, 1971, outlining their major objections as well as their proposals regarding income tax amendments so that taxation of credit unions will be fair and equitable. Only then will the government provide credit unions the opportunity to continue their worthwhile role of great service to people who have joined them in order to help themselves, and of providing a much needed service to their fellow Canadians which is not offered by other financial institutions.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize, also, that credit unions are a unique agency form of collective enterprise. They have an unusual personal, owner-customer relationship with their members, with any surplus earnings, apart from necessary provincial statutory reserves, being allocated to the members. This feature is certainly distinguishable from the operations of the banking system.
In conclusion, all of us in the House of Commons should take very seriously the representations which have been made to us and to the government by credit unions with respect to the effect of the proposed amendments in the income tax bill. I think it is imperative that the Minister of Finance announce without delay amendments favourable to credit unions. I am hopeful that our appeals to the minister will achieve a result which will enable credit unions to continue their great service to the people of Canada and to the economy of our country.

From this side of the House, the hon. members for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair), Kam-loops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand), Gloucester (Mr. Breau) and Okanagan-Boundary (Mr. Howard), among others, all made a point of bringing the views of the credit union and caisses populaires movements to the government's attention in an effective way. I have the impression that it was referred to by some of the 36 opposition members who have so far taken part in the debate. Most of those who dealt with credit unions and caisses populaires also dealt with the related, although not identical, views of the cooperative movement.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and I met here on August 11 with a large delegation from the Co-operative Union of Canada and Le Conseil Canadien de la Co-operation, as well as several of their constituent organizations. On September 20, the Minister of Finance met representatives of Les Federations Des Caisses Populaires and the National Association of Canadian Credit Unions upon his return from the Group of Ten meeting in London. These associations have discussed their views at length with officials of the finance department.
I would like to reward the Canadian Press writer who has stayed here so long waiting for a big news story. However, I can only say at this time that they have done a very effective job of bringing their views to the government's attention and that these views are being seriously considered. What, if any, changes the government deems

maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED PRESSURE BY BANKS TO ACCEPT CREDIT CARDS
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED PRESSURE BY BANKS TO ACCEPT CREDIT CARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the sitting I asked a question to the hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and I drew his attention on the fact that some finance companies and banks are exerting pressure on people to have them accept Chargex credit cards. Even if these people do not ask for these cards, they receive one or are urged by mail to accept one. And even if these financial institutions receive no answer, they send these cards to people thus inviting them to spend without measure. They enclose pamphlets detailing all possibilities for people to travel and for the housewife to buy all kinds of things; however they do not talk about the reimbursement of the money thus advanced. There is hardly a mention about an interest of 18 per cent that will be charged to the client's account.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a rather high handed way of forcing people to accept such credit cards, inviting them to spend more, when we know to which extend such advertisings can be harassing to consumers. Through all kinds of ways, people are sometimes urged to spend much more than they can afford. The advertising is skillfully
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
designed to create the illusion that all kinds of goods can be brought with no obligation to pay and in due course the bills are sent and you have to pay up.
Mr. Speaker, I object to such procedures and I call upon the hon. minister to enact a departmental order or bring forward legislation making it illegal for such companies, whether Simpsons-Sears, Eaton's or others, to force those credit cards on people.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED PRESSURE BY BANKS TO ACCEPT CREDIT CARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can offer complete assurance that no one can be forced to accept a credit card issued by a bank or any other institution. Anyone who is sent a credit card and did not ask for or does not want it is under no obligation to accept or use the card. His best course of action is to destroy any credit cards he does not want.
A number of provinces have specific legislation which relieves consumers of any liability arising from unsolicited credit cards unless they accept their terms and conditions. The government hopes that such legislation will be adopted by all the provinces. If there is any evidence whatsoever that individuals are being pressured to accept credit cards, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) would very much like to have that evidence.
